relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: Gilboa becomes a landscape of flight and death.
Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchi-shua die as sons and persons, not merely pieces of Saul's collapse.
Saul is wounded and overwhelmed under the archers.
Fearing torture, Saul asks another man to kill him; the man refuses, and Saul falls on his sword.
The armor-bearer also dies, a tragedy rather than loyalty's highest form.
The Chronicler compresses the royal household into one catastrophic ending.
Towns empty as civilians flee and Philistines occupy abandoned homes.
The victors return to strip the dead.
Saul's body and weapons become imperial-religious propaganda.
His head and armor are displayed inside Philistine sacred space.
Jabesh-gilead hears and remembers an older bond.
Men travel to recover the bodies, bury the bones, and fast in grief.
The Chronicler interprets Saul's death through disobedience and forbidden consultation, while the endangered medium's humanity must remain visible.
A theological verdict transfers the kingdom to David, but cannot make every detail of Saul's death just or simple.

contemplative_note: The Chronicler wants Saul's ending to explain David's beginning. Grief resists that simplification. Jonathan and his brothers are dead, civilians are displaced, bodies are desecrated, a terrified subordinate dies, and Jabesh fasts. No succession story should rush past the human cost that made the throne available.
